simple: a test that measures how fast something runs, done the same way every time.
analogy: Tomás's stopwatch evenings, if he ran them properly.
precise: a repeatable experiment that applies a defined workload to a system and records a performance metric (time, throughput, latency) together with the conditions of the run.
source: D1 of F2-51 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (benchmarking activities, pitfalls of benchmarking, active benchmarking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a benchmark of one tiny piece of code, such as one loop.
analogy: timing only the omelette, not the whole dinner service.
precise: a benchmark of a small, isolated operation; it is easy to run and easy to get wrong, because the surrounding program, the compiler and the machine's state influence it strongly.
source: D1 of F2-51 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (benchmarking activities, pitfalls of benchmarking, active benchmarking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a run you do first and do not count.
analogy: preheating the stove before the timed omelette.
precise: an untimed execution of the workload before measurement, so that one-time costs (first touch of memory pages, filling caches, loading code, the processor changing its clock speed) do not land in the timed runs.
source: D1 of F2-51 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (benchmarking activities, pitfalls of benchmarking, active benchmarking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F2-51 (run record: lab runs of Listing 5 (noise_quiet.log, noise_busy.log), same toolchain, exit code 0; measurements of a shared cloud virtual machine)

simple: a clock that only ever moves forward at a constant rate, even if someone changes the time of day.
analogy: a stopwatch, not the wall clock that is set forward in spring.
precise: in C++, std::chrono::steady_clock, whose time points never decrease as physical time advances; is_steady is true for it. system_clock follows the wall-clock time and may jump.
source: D2 of F2-51 (ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG21, working draft of the C++ standard (ISO/IEC 14882; tier 1; document number to be recorded): the clause on time utilities (class steady_clock, is_steady) and the clause on program execution (the observable-behaviour rule)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R1 of F2-51 (run record: lab run of Listing 3 (university/labs/F2-51/clockinfo.log), toolchain g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, sanitizer build, exit code 0)

simple: the smallest time step a clock can show you.
analogy: a stopwatch that shows tenths of a second cannot time a 3-millisecond event.
precise: the smallest observable difference between two readings; it is not the same as the clock's declared tick (period), and must be measured.
source: R1 of F2-51 (run record: lab run of Listing 3 (university/labs/F2-51/clockinfo.log), toolchain g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, sanitizer build, exit code 0)

simple: the median is the middle value after sorting; the 90th percentile is the value that 90 % of results are at or below.
analogy: line up all of Tomás's omelette times from fastest to slowest and point at the middle one.
precise: for n sorted values, the median is the value at position (n+1)/2 for odd n (the mean of the two middle values for even n); the nearest-rank p-th percentile is the value at rank ⌈p/100 × n⌉.
source: D4 of F2-51 (MA202 Probability and statistics, chapter F0-63 "Statistics for benchmarks: median, percentiles, outliers" (this university; course card in guide section 5). The definitions used here (median, nearest-rank percentile) are stated and computed in this chapter's worked example and Listing 4) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R5 of F2-51 (run record: lab run of Listing 4 with stats.in (stats.log), sanitizer build, exit code 0)

simple: the same program, run again on the same machine, takes a different time.
analogy: the omelette takes longer when other cooks share the stove.
precise: the spread of repeated measurements of an unchanged workload, caused by everything the program does not control: other processes, interrupts, frequency changes, cache and memory state, timer resolution. In this chapter it is reported as (max − min) / median.
source: D1 of F2-51 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapters on methodology and on benchmarking (benchmarking activities, pitfalls of benchmarking, active benchmarking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F2-51 (run record: lab runs of Listing 5 (noise_quiet.log, noise_busy.log), same toolchain, exit code 0; measurements of a shared cloud virtual machine)

simple: a tiny piece of code that tells the compiler "this value is needed, do not throw away the work that made it".
analogy: Tomás asking to taste the omelette, so the chef must really cook it.
precise: here, bench::keep: a GNU extended-asm statement with no instructions whose input is the value and whose clobber list says "memory"; the compiler must materialise the value and may not delete the computation (dead code elimination, the term of F1-31).
source: D3 of F2-51 (GNU project, "Using the GNU Compiler Collection" (the GCC manual; tier 2; version to match GCC 13.3): sections on optimize options, on extended asm (input operands, the "memory" clobber, volatile) and on function attributes (noinline)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F2-51 (run record: disassembly of the -O2 build of Listing 2 (dce_asm.log), GNU objdump (GNU Binutils for Ubuntu) 2.42, exit code 0)

simple: following a chain where each step tells you where the next step is.
analogy: a treasure hunt in the pantry: each jar has a note with the shelf number of the next jar.
precise: a loop of the form i = next[i], in which every load's address depends on the previous load's value; loads cannot overlap, so the time per step approximates the load latency of the level of the memory hierarchy that holds the working set.
source: D3 of F2-52 (Randal Bryant, David O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the memory hierarchy (locality, the memory mountain, rearranging loops to increase spatial locality, blocking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F2-52 (run record: chase.log: Listing 3, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, -O2, exit code 0; measurements of the build container (AH-23))

simple: swapping which loop is inside and which is outside, so memory is visited in the order it is stored.
analogy: Nadia's switch from plate-by-plate to sauce-by-sauce.
precise: a legal reordering of a loop nest's loops (allowed when it does not change the result) chosen so that the innermost loop has unit stride over the array's storage order.
source: D3 of F2-52 (Randal Bryant, David O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the memory hierarchy (locality, the memory mountain, rearranging loops to increase spatial locality, blocking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: cutting a big job into small square pieces that fit on the shelf, and finishing each piece before starting the next.
analogy: working on one corner of the banquet table with the few trays that fit on the shelf.
precise: splitting the iteration space of a loop nest into blocks (tiles) whose data fits in a chosen cache level, so that lines brought in for one tile are reused before they are evicted.
source: D3 of F2-52 (Randal Bryant, David O'Hallaron, "Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on the memory hierarchy (locality, the memory mountain, rearranging loops to increase spatial locality, blocking)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F2-52 (run record: transpose.log: Listing 4, same toolchain, -O2, exit code 0)

simple: a tool that runs your program on a pretend computer and counts every cache hit and miss.
analogy: a clerk who writes down every trip of the pantry runner.
precise: a Valgrind tool that executes the program on a synthetic CPU, simulating the instruction cache, first-level data cache and last-level cache (with --cache-sim=yes) and attributing references and misses to functions and source lines; its counts are of its own cache model, not of the real hardware.
source: D4 of F2-52 (Valgrind developers, "Valgrind User Manual", chapter "Cachegrind: a high-precision tracing profiler" (tier 2; version 3.22.0 as installed). The HTML manual is not installed in the container (its folder held only images); the options used (--cache-sim, --branch-sim, --cachegrind-out-file) were checked against valgrind --tool=cachegrind --help printed in this build, and the event names against cg_annotate's own header in R3) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F2-52 (run record: traverse.log (Listing 2, timing) and traverse_cg.log (Listing 2 under valgrind-3.22.0 Cachegrind with --cache-sim=yes, then cg_annotate), exit code 0)

simple: one instruction that does the same thing to several numbers at once.
analogy: the eight-spout ladle.
precise: a form of data-level parallelism in which one instruction operates on all elements (lanes) of a vector register; on x86-64, the SSE, AVX/AVX2 and AVX-512 instruction families operate on 128-, 256- and 512-bit registers (4, 8 and 16 single-precision floats).
source: D1 of F2-53 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual" (tier 1; version to be recorded): volume 1 chapters on SSE, AVX, FMA and AVX-512 programming (register widths, packed versus scalar instructions); volume 2 instruction pages for ADDPS/ADDSS and VFMADD…PS) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D5 of F2-53 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on data-level parallelism in vector, SIMD and GPU architectures) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a wide register that holds several numbers side by side; each slot is a lane.
analogy: the row of cups under the spouts; each cup is a lane.
precise: an architectural register of 128 (xmm), 256 (ymm) or 512 (zmm) bits on x86-64; a lane is one element position. (HW301 uses "lane" for one thread of a GPU warp, F1-57; the idea is related, the mechanism differs.)
source: D1 of F2-53 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual" (tier 1; version to be recorded): volume 1 chapters on SSE, AVX, FMA and AVX-512 programming (register widths, packed versus scalar instructions); volume 2 instruction pages for ADDPS/ADDSS and VFMADD…PS) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the compiler rewriting your ordinary loop to use SIMD instructions.
analogy: the translator noticing that the recipe says "fill each cup" and writing "use the wide ladle".
precise: a compiler transformation (vectorisation, F1-31) that turns loop iterations into vector operations when it can prove this preserves the program's meaning; in GCC it is enabled at -O3 and, in a cheaper form, at -O2, and reported with -fopt-info-vec.
source: D3 of F2-53 (GNU project, "Using the GNU Compiler Collection" (GCC 13 manual; tier 2): sections on optimize options (-ftree-vectorize, -ffast-math, -fassociative-math), developer options (-fopt-info), x86 options (-march), function attributes (target), other built-ins (__builtin_cpu_supports) and restricted pointers) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F2-53 (run record: vec_base.log, vec_native.log: vectoriser reports for Listing 1, same toolchain, exit code 0)

simple: a function that the compiler turns into one particular machine instruction.
analogy: writing "wide ladle" in the recipe yourself instead of hoping the translator does it.
precise: a compiler-provided function, declared in a header such as <immintrin.h>, that maps to a specific instruction; in GCC 13, _mm256_fmadd_ps is defined in fmaintrin.h as a call to the built-in __builtin_ia32_vfmaddps256.
source: H1 of F2-53 (GCC 13 x86 intrinsic headers as installed in the build container (Ubuntu package libgcc-13-dev 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1), read in this build: avxintrin.h (_mm256_set1_ps, _mm256_loadu_ps, _mm256_storeu_ps, _mm256_add_ps, _mm256_broadcast_ss), fmaintrin.h (_mm256_fmadd_ps, defined as __builtin_ia32_vfmaddps256), avx512fintrin.h (the _mm512_ forms used in F2-56). Tier 2 (the compiler project's own header); read in this build); D2 of F2-53 (Intel, "Intel Intrinsics Guide" (tier 1; version to be recorded): entries for _mm256_set1_ps, _mm256_loadu_ps, _mm256_storeu_ps, _mm256_fmadd_ps) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one instruction that computes a × b + c.
analogy: stirring while pouring, in one movement.
precise: an operation computing a × b + c with a single rounding at the end (IEEE 754 fusedMultiplyAdd); x86-64 provides it in the FMA extension (vfmadd…ps instructions). It counts as two floating-point operations in FLOP rates.
source: D1 of F2-53 (Intel, "Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual" (tier 1; version to be recorded): volume 1 chapters on SSE, AVX, FMA and AVX-512 programming (register widths, packed versus scalar instructions); volume 2 instruction pages for ADDPS/ADDSS and VFMADD…PS) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D4 of F2-53 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE 754; tier 1; edition to be recorded): rounding of each operation, fusedMultiplyAdd; and David Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991; tier 5) on non-associativity. Titles only — not opened during this build (dossier gate G1 open)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: combining many numbers into one, such as a sum or a maximum.
analogy: pouring all the cups back into one pot.
precise: a loop that accumulates values with an associative operation into a single result; vectorising it means keeping several partial results (one per lane) and combining them at the end, which changes the order of operations.
source: D5 of F2-53 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on data-level parallelism in vector, SIMD and GPU architectures) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: adding the same float numbers in a different order, which can give a slightly different answer.
analogy: tipping sand and pebbles into a scale in a different order changes which grains the scale can still show.
precise: floating-point addition is commutative but not associative, because every addition rounds; (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ. A compiler may reorder floating-point operations only when allowed (for example by -ffast-math or -fassociative-math in GCC).
source: D4 of F2-53 (IEEE, "IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic" (IEEE 754; tier 1; edition to be recorded): rounding of each operation, fusedMultiplyAdd; and David Goldberg, "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1991; tier 5) on non-associativity. Titles only — not opened during this build (dossier gate G1 open)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D3 of F2-53 (GNU project, "Using the GNU Compiler Collection" (GCC 13 manual; tier 2): sections on optimize options (-ftree-vectorize, -ffast-math, -fassociative-math), developer options (-fopt-info), x86 options (-march), function attributes (target), other built-ins (__builtin_cpu_supports) and restricted pointers) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F2-53 (run record: order.log: Listing 4, sanitizer build, exit code 0)

simple: an if whose direction depends on the values being processed, not on the loop counter.
analogy: the guest's order.
precise: a conditional branch whose outcome is a function of loaded data; it is predictable only if the data has a pattern the predictor can learn.
source: D1 of F2-54 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on instruction-level parallelism (dynamic branch prediction, correlating and tournament predictors, speculation)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F2-54 (run record: branches_cmov.log, branches_jump.log: Listing 1 in the two builds, exit code 0; measurements of a shared cloud virtual machine (AH-23))

simple: code that computes both possibilities, or a mask, and picks the result with arithmetic instead of jumping.
analogy: preparing the plate so that it fits every order, with one ingredient switched on or off.
precise: code in which no conditional jump depends on the data; the selection is done with a conditional move / select instruction, masks (-(b >= 128) & b), or SIMD compare-and-blend. It trades possible mispredictions for always doing the work of both paths.
source: D1 of F2-54 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): the chapter on instruction-level parallelism (dynamic branch prediction, correlating and tournament predictors, speculation)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F2-54 (run record: asm_cmov.log, asm_jump.log: disassembly with GNU objdump (GNU Binutils for Ubuntu) 2.42, exit code 0)

simple: the compiler turning your if into branchless code by itself.
analogy: the translator rewriting "if the guest wants cheese, add cheese" as "add the cheese amount the guest asked for (possibly none)".
precise: a compiler transformation that replaces a conditional branch around simple code with predicated or conditional-move instructions; GCC's -fif-conversion and -fif-conversion2 passes do this and are switched off by the -fno- forms used in this chapter's "jump" build.
source: D3 of F2-54 (GNU project, "Using the GNU Compiler Collection" (GCC 13 manual; tier 2): optimize options -fif-conversion, -fif-conversion2; other built-ins (__builtin_expect)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R3 of F2-54 (run record: asm_cmov.log, asm_jump.log: disassembly with GNU objdump (GNU Binutils for Ubuntu) 2.42, exit code 0)

simple: a tool that pretends to be a branch predictor and counts its wrong guesses.
analogy: a clerk who notes every guess the first cook makes and whether it was right.
precise: with --branch-sim=yes, Cachegrind counts executed conditional branches (Bc) and their mispredictions (Bcm), and indirect branches (Bi, Bim), using its own simple predictor model, per function.
source: D4 of F2-54 (Valgrind developers, "Valgrind User Manual", chapter "Cachegrind: a high-precision tracing profiler" (tier 2; version 3.22.0 as installed): branch simulation, the events Bc, Bcm, Bi, Bim) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R4 of F2-54 (run record: cg_sorted.log, cg_shuffled.log: valgrind-3.22.0 Cachegrind with --branch-sim=yes, then cg_annotate, on the jump build; exit code 0; simulated, not hardware, counts)

simple: a profiler that adds counting code to every function or instruction so that nothing is missed (SP202 calls the instruction-counting kind an instruction-count profiler).
analogy: the clerk who logs every action.
precise: profiling by inserting code at compile time (gprof's -pg call counting) or at run time (Valgrind's dynamic binary translation in Callgrind) that counts events exactly; complete and deterministic, but it slows the program, often many times, and may change its behaviour.
source: D3 of F2-55 (GNU project, "GNU gprof" manual (tier 2; GNU Binutils 2.42 as installed): flat profile, call graph, -pg) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D4 of F2-55 (Valgrind developers, "Valgrind User Manual", chapter "Callgrind: a call-graph generating cache and branch prediction profiler" (tier 2; version 3.22.0 as installed): inclusive and self cost, --toggle-collect, callgrind_annotate) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: self cost is what a function does itself; inclusive cost adds everything it calls.
analogy: the time the head cook spends cooking, versus that time plus all the jobs she hands to helpers.
precise: self (exclusive) cost is the cost of instructions inside the function's own body; inclusive cost is self cost plus the inclusive cost of its callees along the observed call graph.
source: D4 of F2-55 (Valgrind developers, "Valgrind User Manual", chapter "Callgrind: a call-graph generating cache and branch prediction profiler" (tier 2; version 3.22.0 as installed): inclusive and self cost, --toggle-collect, callgrind_annotate) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the map of which function calls which.
analogy: the chain of who hands work to whom in the kitchen.
precise: a directed graph whose nodes are functions and whose edges are observed calls, annotated with call counts and costs; gprof and Callgrind both build one.
source: D3 of F2-55 (GNU project, "GNU gprof" manual (tier 2; GNU Binutils 2.42 as installed): flat profile, call graph, -pg) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); D4 of F2-55 (Valgrind developers, "Valgrind User Manual", chapter "Callgrind: a call-graph generating cache and branch prediction profiler" (tier 2; version 3.22.0 as installed): inclusive and self cost, --toggle-collect, callgrind_annotate) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a counter inside the processor that counts events such as cycles, instructions or cache misses.
analogy: a tally counter fixed to each oven door, clicking every time it opens.
precise: a programmable register in the CPU's performance monitoring unit that counts a selected micro-architectural event; Linux exposes counters through the perf_event_open system call, used by the perf tool. Availability inside virtual machines depends on the hypervisor.
source: D5 of F2-55 (Linux kernel man-pages project, "perf_event_open(2)" manual page, and the perf tool's documentation (tier 2)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open); R2 of F2-55 (run record: counters.log: Listing 1, sanitizer build, exit code 0; hardware events errno 2, software events counted)

simple: a change that makes the program slower than before.
analogy: a new kitchen rule that adds a step to every dish.
precise: a measured, reproducible increase in a performance metric (time, instructions, memory) between two versions, under the same workload and environment.
source: D1 of F2-55 (Brendan Gregg, "Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud" (tier 3; edition to be recorded): methodology chapter (scientific method, the USE method), CPU chapter (profiling, sampling, counters)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much calculation a program does for each byte it moves to or from memory.
analogy: how many cooking steps each crate of ingredients receives.
precise: the ratio of floating-point operations to bytes of memory traffic, in FLOP/byte; which traffic is counted (DRAM, a cache level; compulsory only or measured) must be stated.
source: D1 of F2-56 (Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman, David Patterson, "Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures", Communications of the ACM (curriculum item 75; tier 1): the model, ridge point, ceilings, operational intensity) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a chart that shows the fastest a kernel can possibly run on a machine, given how much calculation it does per byte.
analogy: the kitchen's limit: the stove's or the pantry door's, whichever is lower for that dish.
precise: attainable performance = min(peak FLOP/s, arithmetic intensity × peak bandwidth), drawn on log–log axes as a slanted line (memory roof) meeting a flat line (compute roof).
source: D1 of F2-56 (Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman, David Patterson, "Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures", Communications of the ACM (curriculum item 75; tier 1): the model, ridge point, ceilings, operational intensity) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the intensity where the two limits meet.
analogy: the dish for which the stove and the door are equally busy.
precise: peak FLOP/s divided by peak bandwidth (FLOP/byte); kernels to its left are memory-bound, to its right compute-bound.
source: D1 of F2-56 (Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman, David Patterson, "Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures", Communications of the ACM (curriculum item 75; tier 1): the model, ridge point, ceilings, operational intensity) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: limited by moving data, or limited by calculating.
analogy: the salad (door-limited) and the stew (stove-limited).
precise: a kernel is memory-bound if intensity × bandwidth is below peak FLOP/s, compute-bound otherwise; the label describes the roof above it, not how close it runs to that roof.
source: D1 of F2-56 (Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman, David Patterson, "Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures", Communications of the ACM (curriculum item 75; tier 1): the model, ridge point, ceilings, operational intensity) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the roof's height above a kernel: the best it could do.
analogy: the most plates per hour this dish could reach in this kitchen.
precise: min(peak, AI × bandwidth) for that kernel's intensity; "percent of roof" = measured / attainable.
source: D1 of F2-56 (Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman, David Patterson, "Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures", Communications of the ACM (curriculum item 75; tier 1): the model, ridge point, ceilings, operational intensity) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: multiplying two matrices of single-precision numbers.
analogy: the stew: lots of cooking per ingredient.
precise: single-precision general matrix multiply, C = αAB + βC in the BLAS interface; here α = 1, β = 0, row-major, M × K times K × N, 2MNK floating-point operations.
source: D4 of F2-56 (Kazushige Goto, Robert van de Geijn, "Anatomy of High-Performance Matrix Multiplication", ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software (tier 1): blocking for caches, packing, the register micro-kernel; and the BLAS SGEMM interface) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: computing a small block of the answer entirely in registers, reusing every loaded number many times.
analogy: keeping a few pans on the stove and adding to all of them from each crate before fetching the next.
precise: an innermost kernel that keeps an MR × NR block of C in vector registers and, for each k, loads NR values of B and MR values of A to perform MR × NR fused multiply-adds; here MR = 6, NR = 16 with AVX2.
source: D4 of F2-56 (Kazushige Goto, Robert van de Geijn, "Anatomy of High-Performance Matrix Multiplication", ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software (tier 1): blocking for caches, packing, the register micro-kernel; and the BLAS SGEMM interface) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
